title: US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
detail:
US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
Lockridge Okoth
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 3:56 PM MST 2 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
^DJI
CL=F
^NDX

Wall Street appeared ready to recover from October's $2 trillion technology stock wipeout on Monday. Within hours, roughly $700 billion in fresh market gains had evaporated.

The S&P 500 surged as much as 1.1% in morning trading before closing down 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1%, extending last week's brutal AI stock selloff.

The reversal came shortly after CNBC host Jim Cramer posted on X:

"Here we go: biggest tech takeout."

He was referring to Marvell's $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. But the timing quickly revived jokes about Cramer's famously mixed market predictions.

Why Did the Stock Market Rally Suddenly Collapse?

The morning optimism came from the Middle East.

Oil prices dropped to $104 as possible US-Iran peace talks raised hopes of cheaper energy and easing inflation.

Stocks initially jumped. The Nasdaq 100 gained around 1.3%, while the Dow climbed more than 1%.

But investors soon returned to the same concern that erased more than $2 trillion from the Nasdaq 100 during October: How much longer can Big Tech keep spending billions on AI without delivering sufficient returns?

Oracle plunged nearly 9% after announcing plans to raise $20 billion through stock and bond sales to fund its AI expansion. Marvell lost almost 13%.

White House Says AI Has Plenty of Money

Meanwhile, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett dismissed fears of an AI financing crisis.

"There's so much cash in the ecosystem that I think that people should be reassured," Hassett said.

Interestingly, nearly 70% of S&P 500 companies finished higher. The weakness remained concentrated in major technology stocks.

As for Cramer's supposed curse, the Inverse Cramer ETF, designed to bet against his recommendations, lost 15% before closing in 2024.

Investors now face Tuesday's US midterm elections and Friday's jobs report, with confidence in the AI trade already shaken.

title: Tech selloff: are AI spending concerns justified?
detail:
Tech selloff: are AI spending concerns justified?
Dan McEvoy
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 7:51 AM MST 4 min read
^NDX
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Credit: Westend61 via Getty Images

Concerns over the scale of capital expenditure on artificial intelligence by the industry's biggest tech companies have seen trillions of dollars wiped off their combined market valuation.

Between its peak on 6 October and the end of the month, the Nasdaq 100 dropped by more than 9%. Estimates put the market value of these losses at around $5 trillion.

"For three years, tech giants only had to announce investment in artificial intelligence (AI) to be rewarded by the stock market," Grégoire Kounowski, head of advisory at wealth manager Norman K. observed. "That is no longer the case. The third-quarter earnings season marks a turning point: investors now want to know when this spending will pay off, and how it will be financed."

AI's biggest names – especially hardware providers like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) – have seen surging profits and their market capitalisations boom as spending on AI infrastructure has soared.

But investors are becoming increasingly sceptical over the sustainability of these increased AI profits, and appear ready to penalise businesses that can't demonstrate clear returns on their AI investments.

Has AI cannibalised Google Search?

The rout began when Google's parent company Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) reported its results for Q3 of 2026 on 28 October. Diluted earnings per share (EPS) fell 26.1% year-on-year to $2.12 – well short of analyst forecasts of $3.02.

Although Google Search volumes reached record levels, revenue growth in the segment slowed to 12% from 17% in the previous quarter – suggesting that Google's own AI overviews may be hurting its ability to monetise its core product.

Alphabet's shares tumbled by 12.6% the following day and lost a further 1.4% on 30 October.

"Alphabet saw $463 billion wiped off its market value [in a single day]," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at wealth manager AJ Bell. "Alphabet's results could go down in history as a major turning point in the AI story. They showed another quarter of cash burn and that AI summaries on search were affecting advertising revenue. The bear case many had dismissed is now becoming a reality."

Alphabet was joined by Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) which fell by 28.6% on 30 October, following an alarmingly bleak forecast for Q4 accompanying its Q3 results the previous evening.

"The gigantic declines we've seen this week in shares such as Alphabet and Intel suggest that investor sentiment has been turned on its head," said Coatsworth. "Current price action implies tech investors want to jump off the treadmill rather than slow it down."

AMD Just Dropped 16% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Dean Drobot via Canva
Key Takeaways

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) declined 16% in the month through October 23, while Intel (INTC) fell 29% and the Nasdaq 100 lost 5%, as investors questioned the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.

AMD dropped 10.9% on October 30, closing near $505 after Intel's disappointing outlook intensified concerns about semiconductor demand.

TIKR's October 21 consensus estimates projected AMD's normalized earnings per share to rise from approximately $8 in 2026 to $16 in 2027, supported by expected growth in AI accelerators and data center infrastructure.

AMD traded at approximately 46x forward earnings as of October 22, above its five-year average of 35x, making the decline a potential long-term buying opportunity rather than an outright bargain.

What Happened?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock fell 16% in the month through October 23, closing around $517 as concerns about AI infrastructure financing and elevated semiconductor valuations weighed on investor sentiment.

The decline was smaller than Intel (INTC) stock's 29% drop and considerably worse than the Nasdaq 100's 5% pullback, highlighting growing uncertainty over whether AI infrastructure spending could support chipmakers' valuations.

Concerns intensified on October 8 after a Financial Times report indicated that OpenAI's annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion, approximately $20 billion below figures previously circulating in the market.

The discrepancy, partly related to revenue accounting methods, raised questions about the financing capacity of major AI customers. OpenAI is particularly important to AMD because of its multigigawatt GPU supply agreement.

Further pressure emerged on October 14 when weakness in CoreWeave's bonds intensified concerns about financing expensive data centers. On October 16, all 30 Philadelphia Semiconductor Index constituents declined, extending the index's losing streak to eight sessions, its longest since 2008.

AMD also faced scrutiny over its involvement in customer financing. On October 13, the company signed a credit-support agreement involving Fermi's 222-megawatt Texas data center campus, which is intended to accommodate AMD-powered infrastructure.

AMD has also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic and issued performance-based warrants allowing OpenAI and Meta to purchase up to 160 million AMD shares each, subject to GPU deployment and other conditions.

Baird technology strategist Ted Mortonson captured investor concerns on Bloomberg Surveillance, saying his clients "hate the bank of AMD," highlighting skepticism about chipmakers supporting the financing of their own customers.

Key Takeaways

Astera Labs fell 11% on Friday, nearly four times the Nasdaq Composite's 2.9% drop, on AI spending worries that didn't come from Astera.

To keep the $1.91 billion revenue estimate for 2026 intact, the November 3 report needs a fourth-quarter guide of $648 million to $668 million.

About half of the margin slide comes from a non-cash Amazon warrant charge. Hardware mix is the other half, and it's the part to watch.

At 46x forward earnings, against a one-year average of 72x, delivering the plan should be enough.

Astera Labs (ALAB:NASDAQ) stock fell 11% on Friday, October 30, nearly four times the Nasdaq Composite's 2.9% drop. Alphabet (GOOGL) had just reported disappointing search results, Amazon (AMZN) had signaled heavier AI spending, and Intel (INTC) had warned on cash burn. Together they revived doubts about when all that AI spending pays off. The Nasdaq 100 briefly traded 10% below its October 6 record, in correction territory, before closing 9.1% off the high.

None of that news came from Astera. The company reports its third quarter after the close on Tuesday, November 3, with the stock already marked down. That helps on revenue, where the bar is clear and Astera keeps clearing it. It helps less on margin, where management has already guided to its lowest number in at least three years.

Revenue Has a Clear Bar

Analysts expect Astera's revenue to more than double again in 2026, to $1.91 billion, then climb to $2.98 billion in 2027 and $3.82 billion in 2028.

ALAB Revenue Estimates: FY2024-FY2028 (TIKR)

That 2027 figure stood at $1.34 billion a year ago, and management has earned the upgrades. Revenue beat the top of guidance in each of the last three quarters. The third-quarter guide of $540 million to $560 million sits about 40% above the second quarter's $392.4 million at the midpoint. Astera also expects Scorpio fabric switches to become its largest product family this quarter, one quarter ahead of plan.

So the number that matters on Tuesday is the fourth-quarter guide. Start with the $1.91 billion consensus, then subtract the $700.8 million Astera booked in the first half and the third-quarter range. That leaves $648 million to $668 million for the fourth quarter.
